title: Single-Parent Households and Their Resilience in the Works of Ruskin Bond and R. K. Narayan: Not Always Defective, Often Successful
content: Indian family structure increasingly includes single-parent households. However, children's literature in English from India often leaves out this fact. In order to understand what kinds of literary representation single-parent households receive in children's literature, this study focuses on two of the most popular Indian English authors, Ruskin Bond and R. K. Narayan. Qualitative thematic analysis of a purposive sample of one novel and seven short stories by Bond and three short stories and one novel by Narayan is conducted within the context of sociological studies of family structure and child development. The analysis shows that both authors present single-parent households not as a defective structure but as a source of either care and safety or a lack thereof, which defines a child's destiny: an attentive lone parent gives the child security, while a neglecting or authoritarian carer makes a child run away and build a family of choice among peers. Besides, children in works of Bond and Narayan learn to take care of their lone parent and develop early due to this. Finally, both authors rely on personal experience of having lost one of the parents. The paper presents a typology of four household types found in these texts: the sustaining lone parent, the strained lone parent, the neglectful or hostile carer, and surrogate or communal care. In conclusion, the paper points to the need for Indian children's literature that reflects the diversity of modern Indian families.
